newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ to win more independence in monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: BOJ to win more independence in monetary policy.

text.p: The Bank of Japan, long criticised for having less independence than other major central banks, will win some new freedoms but fail to shake off all government influence under a plan issued on Thursday.

The Financial System Research Council submitted its final report on reforms to the finance minister. The recommendations will form the basis for bills to be submitted to parliament in early March and changes would take effect on April 1 next year.

"The report appears to have taken the BOJ's independence a step or two forward, but in reality, I don't think things have changed all that much," said Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute Corp.

The plan, which aims to free the central bank from the grip of the powerful Ministry of Finance (MOF), is part of an overhaul of the government and Japan's financial system promoted by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

Hashimoto, himself a former finance minister, hopes to reduce the authority of MOF, which has come under fire for its handling of Japan's banking crisis and embarrassing scandals involving its senior officials.
The plan calls for a number of changes to bring more freedom to the central bank:
-- The government could only request the BOJ's policy-making board to postpone monetary policy decisions, while at present it can order the central bank to do so.
-- Two government representatives who are currently members of the BOJ's policy-making board could attend meetings "only when necessary".
-- The finance minister would continue to approve BOJ budgets, but only for costs other than those relating to money supply and monetary policy.
-- The minister would no longer have the authority to directly carry out inspections of the BOJ. Any checks on whether the BOJ has broken any laws or regulations would be made by BOJ auditors.
"I think we've come a long way (in securing independence)," said Yoshio Suzuki, a former BOJ executive and now a member of parliament.
But he said rules were needed to decide when it was "necessary" for government officials to attend policy-making meetings.
Takagi of Fuji Research said that in order for the BOJ to maintain stability in Japan's financial system, the central bank should have been given more independence to deal with financial crises.

Under the proposals, special BOJ loans to troubled banks would be made at the request of MOF. But the BOJ would be able to make special low-interest loans without collateral to banks without consulting the government if they faced a temporary liquidity shortage, such as when computers malfunctioned.
In exchange for its independence, the BOJ would report to parliament twice a year, instead of once a year as at present.
The policy-making board would also make public the minutes of its meetings after a set time.

BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita, asked at a news conference on Thursday if the proposals would restrict the BOJ's independence in monetary policy, said various efforts had been made to increase the BOJ's independence.
"The proposals could help the BOJ's efforts to reform itself towards the 21st century, and we highly evaluate them," he said.
